name: Superior sagittal sinus
summary: The largest dural venous sinus, running in the attached edge of the falx from the crista galli to the internal occipital protuberance, where it turns (usually to the right) into a transverse sinus at the confluence. It receives the superior cerebral (bridging) veins from the convexity, the lateral lacunae with their arachnoid granulations that return CSF to the blood, and emissary and diploic veins. Its thrombosis, the commonest cerebral venous thrombosis, causes headache, seizures, bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic infarcts and raised intracranial pressure, and it is the sinus invaded by parasagittal meningiomas.

anatomy.location: Midline along the vault in the upper margin of the falx, triangular in section, enlarging posteriorly; lateral lacunae extend into the dura beside it in the parietal region.

function: Drainage of the superior and medial cerebral cortex and the diploë; absorption of CSF through the arachnoid granulations in its lacunae.

arteries: (venous structure) drains territories of the cerebral arteries

bestView.label: triangular sinus at the top of the falx
sinus along the vault from front to back

imaging.normalAppearance: A triangular dark flow void at the vertex on coronal T2 and a dense triangle enhancing on contrast CT (the empty delta sign is a filling defect in thrombosis); MR or CT venography shows it as a continuous channel. Absent flow, T1-bright thrombus and bilateral parasagittal edema are the thrombosis triad.

pathology.finding: Absent flow in the sinus on MR venography, dense clot on CT (cord sign) and empty delta on contrast CT, with bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic venous infarcts.
pathology.timing: Thrombus is isointense on T1 in the first days, bright from day 5 to ~4 weeks

pathology.finding: Enhancing mass narrowing or occluding the sinus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CT venography or MR venography with T1/SWI for thrombus

lesionEffects.deficit: Headache, papilledema and raised intracranial pressure
lesionEffects.mechanism: Impaired venous outflow and CSF absorption

examination: Seizure history; risk factors: pregnancy, contraceptives, dehydration, infection, thrombophilia
pearls: Headache with bilateral or unusual hemorrhagic infarcts that do not fit an arterial territory is venous thrombosis until proven otherwise
A dense triangle at the vertex on plain CT in a headache patient should prompt a venogram
